title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 144 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 702–713 (Night 144, continuing directly from nights-143), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 144 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. At Baghdad a plundered merchant appeals to King Rūmzān and Kān Mā Kān; they ride out, rout the Bedouin raiders and restore his goods, and he turns out to be the merchant who once bought Nuzhat al-Zamān and gave her to her brother Sharrukān. She receives him with gifts. Of the three captured bandit chiefs, a Bedouin tells how he once kidnapped a girl in Jerusalem and sold her in Damascus — and Nuzhat al-Zamān knows him as her own kidnapper and draws a sword on him. To save his life he tells a stranger story: how he, Ḥammād, came upon a young warrior and his sister alone in the desert, demanded the girl, saw his companions killed one by one in single combat, was spared and feasted by the youth, ʿAbbād ibn Tamīm ibn Thaʿlaba — and then beheaded him in his sleep, while the sister lamented in verse and fell on her sword. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّاكَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-fourth night,
sentences.n: The print runs lammā and kānat together as one word, فلماكانت; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُمَا اتَّفَقَا عَلَى أَنَّ كُلَّوَاحِدٍ يَحْكُمُ يَوْمًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahumā ittafaqā ʿalā anna kulla wāḥidin yaḥkumu yawman
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the two-of-them agreed on that each-one should rule a day.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the two of them agreed that each should rule for a day in turn.
sentences.n: The new night opens by repeating the agreement on which the last one closed. ittafaqā ʿalā, “the two agreed upon”, a dual verb. kulla wāḥidin is accusative as the subject of anna; the print again runs kull wāḥid together as one word, كلواحد.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَوْلَمُوا الْوَلَائِمَ وَذَبَحُوا الذَّبَائِحَ وَزَادَتْ بِهِمُ الْأَفْرَاحُ وَأَقَامُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ مُدَّةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma awlamū al-walāʾima wa-dhabaḥū al-dhabāʾiḥa wa-zādat bihimu al-afrāḥu wa-aqāmū ʿalā dhālika muddatan mina al-zamāni
sentences.l: Then they banqueted the banquets and slaughtered the slaughter-beasts, and the rejoicings increased with them; and they remained on that a space of the time.
sentences.i: Then they held feasts and slaughtered beasts for the table, and their rejoicing grew; and so they continued for some time.
sentences.n: awlamū al-walāʾima, “they feasted the feasts”, and dhabaḥū al-dhabāʾiḥa, “they slaughtered the slaughterings”: each verb takes an object from its own root, a favourite figure of the storyteller. walīma is a feast, especially a wedding feast. aqāma ʿalā, “to remain in (a state)”.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذَلِكَ وَالسُّلْطَانُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَقْطَعُ لَيْلَهُ مَعَ بِنْتِ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-al-sulṭānu Kāna Mā Kāna yaqṭaʿu laylahu maʿa binti ʿammihi Qaḍā Fakān
sentences.l: All that, and the sultan Kān Mā Kān was cutting-through his night with the daughter of his paternal-uncle, Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.i: And all this while Sultan Kān Mā Kān spent his nights with his cousin Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.n: kullu dhālika wa-…, “all that, while …”: a colloquial way of saying that something went on alongside. qaṭaʿa al-layl, “to cut through the night”, to pass it. bint ʿamm, “daughter of a paternal uncle”, the cousin who in Arab custom is the first-choice bride.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةِ بَيْنَمَاهُمْ قَاعِدُونَ فَرْحَانُونَ بِهَذَا الْأَمْرِ وَإِصْلَاحِ الشَّأْنِ إِذْ ظَهَرَ لَهُمْ غُبَارٌ قَدْ عَلَا وَطَارَ حَتَّى سَدَّ الْأَقْطَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda tilka al-muddati baynamā hum qāʿidūna farḥānūna bi-hādhā al-amri wa-iṣlāḥi al-shaʾni idh ẓahara lahum ghubārun qad ʿalā wa-ṭāra ḥattā sadda al-aqṭāra
sentences.l: And after that space, while they were sitting, glad at this matter and the setting-right of the affair, lo, there appeared to them a dust that had risen and flown until it blocked the horizons.
sentences.i: After that time, as they sat rejoicing over this arrangement and the setting in order of their affairs, a cloud of dust appeared before them; it rose and flew until it blotted out the horizon.
sentences.n: The print runs baynamā and hum together, بينماهم; the spacing is kept. baynamā … idh, “while … suddenly”, the stock frame for an interruption. farḥān, “glad”, with the plural farḥānūn, is colloquial (Classical fariḥ); qāʿid, “sitting”, likewise. The rising dust is rhymed: ṭāra, “flew”, with al-aqṭāra, “the horizons”. The hamza in الشأن is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَتَى إِلَيْهِمْ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ صَارِخٌ يَسْتَغِيثُ وَهُوَ يَصِيحُ وَيَقُولُ يَا مُلُوكَ الزَّمَانِ كَيْفَ أَسْلَمُ فِي بِلَادِ الْكُفْرِ وَأُنْهَبُ فِي بِلَادِكُمْ وَهِيَ بِلَادُ الْعَدْلِ وَالْأَمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad atā ilayhim mina al-tujjāri ṣārikhun yastaghīthu wa-huwa yaṣīḥu wa-yaqūlu yā mulūka al-zamāni kayfa aslamu fī bilādi al-kufri wa-unhabu fī bilādikum wa-hiya bilādu al-ʿadli wa-al-amāni
sentences.l: And there had come to them, from-among the merchants, a crier calling-for-help, and he shouting and saying: O kings of the time, how am-I-safe in the lands of unbelief and am-plundered in your lands, and they the lands of justice and security?
sentences.i: And there came to them one of the merchants, crying out for help, shouting and saying, “O kings of the age, how is it that I go safe in the lands of the unbelievers, and am plundered in your lands, which are the lands of justice and security?”
sentences.n: The damma on the alif of اُنهب is the print's own, marking the passive unhabu, “I am plundered”. salima, “to be safe, come through unharmed”. istaghātha, “to cry for help”. His cry is rhymed: al-zamān, “the age”, with al-amān, “security”.

sentences.t: فَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-aqbala ʿalayhi al-maliku Rūmzānu wa-saʾalahu ʿan ḥālihi
sentences.l: And King Rūmzān turned-towards him and asked him about his state.
sentences.i: King Rūmzān turned to him and asked him what had befallen him.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn one's face to, attend to”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَنَا تَاجِرٌ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ وَلِي غَائِبٌ عَنِ الْأَوْطَانِ مُدَّةً مَدِيدَةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ وَاسْتَغْرَقْتُ فِى الْبِلَادِ نَحْوَ عِشْرِينَ سَنَةً مِنَ الْأَعْوَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu anā tājirun mina al-tujjāri wa-lī ghāʾibun ʿani al-awṭāni muddatan madīdatan mina al-zamāni wa-istaghraqtu fī al-bilādi naḥwa ʿishrīna sanatan mina al-aʿwāmi
sentences.l: And he said to him: I am a merchant of the merchants, and I-have (been) absent from the homelands a long space of the time, and I-have-been-sunk in the lands about twenty years of the years.
sentences.i: He said to him, “I am a merchant, and I have been away from home a long, long while: for some twenty years I have been lost in foreign lands.
sentences.n: wa-lī ghāʾibun, literally “and to me (is) absent”: a colloquial turn, “I have been away”, with lī carrying the sense of time spent. The doubling is the merchant's: muddatan madīdatan, “a long space”, min al-zamān, “of time”; sanatan min al-aʿwām, “years of the years”. awṭān, “homelands”, rhymes with zamān. istaghraqa, “to be immersed, swallowed up”. The print spells fī with ى here.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّ مَعِي كِتَابًا مِنْ مَدِينَةِ دِمَشْقَ كَانَ قَدْ كَتَبَهُ لِي الْمَرْحُومُ الْمَلِكُ شَرْكَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-inna maʿī kitāban min madīnati Dimashqa kāna qad katabahu lī al-marḥūmu al-maliku Sharrukānu
sentences.l: And indeed with me (is) a letter from the city of Damascus, which the late King Sharrukān had written for me.
sentences.i: I have with me a letter from the city of Damascus, written for me by the late King Sharrukān.
sentences.n: al-marḥūm, “the one (God) has had mercy on”, the regular epithet of the dead: “the late”. kāna qad katabahu, pluperfect, “he had written it”.

sentences.t: وَسَبَبُ ذَلِكَ أَنِّي كُنْتُ قَدْأَ هْدَيْتُ إِلَيْهِ جَارِيَةً
sentences.tr: wa-sababu dhālika annī kuntu qad ahdaytu ilayhi jāriyatan
sentences.l: And the cause of that (was) that I had presented to him a slave-girl.
sentences.i: This was because I had once made him a present of a slave-girl.
sentences.n: The print splits ahdaytu, “I presented”, after its first letter, writing قدا هديت; the spacing is kept and the words are pointed as qad ahdaytu. ahdā ilā, “to give as a gift to”. The girl was Nuzhat al-Zamān, bought from a Bedouin and given to her own brother Sharrukān without either knowing who she was.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرُبْتُ مِنْ تِلْكَ الْبِلَادِ وَكَانَ مَعِي مِائَةُ حِمْلٍ مِنْ تُحَفِ الْهِنْدِ وَأَتَيْتُ بِهَا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ الَّتِي هِيَ حَرَمُكُمْ وَمَحَلُّ أَمْنِكُمْ وَعَدْلِكُمْ فَخَرَجَتْ عَلَيْنَا عُرْبَانٌ وَمَعَهُمْ أَكْرَادٌ مُجْتَمِعَةٌ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْبِلَادِ فَقَتَلُوا رِجَالِي وَنَهَبُوا أَمْوَالِي وَهَذَا شَرْحُ حَالِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qarubtu min tilka al-bilādi wa-kāna maʿī miʾatu ḥimlin min tuḥafi al-hindi wa-ataytu bihā ilā Baghdāda allatī hiya ḥaramukum wa-maḥallu amnikum wa-ʿadlikum fa-kharajat ʿalaynā ʿurbānun wa-maʿahum akrādun mujtamiʿatun min jamīʿi al-bilādi fa-qatalū rijālī wa-nahabū amwālī wa-hādhā sharḥu ḥālī
sentences.l: And when I drew-near to those lands, and there was with me a hundred loads of the rarities of India, and I brought them to Baghdad, which is your sanctuary and the place of your security and your justice, there came-out against us Bedouins, and with them Kurds gathered from all the lands; and they killed my men, and plundered my goods; and this is the account of my state.
sentences.i: Now when I drew near to these lands, with a hundred loads of the rarities of India, bringing them to Baghdad, which is your sanctuary and the seat of your security and justice, Bedouins fell upon us, and Kurds with them gathered from every land. They killed my men and plundered my goods. That is my story.”
sentences.n: ʿurbān, a colloquial plural of ʿarab, means the desert Arabs, the Bedouin; akrād, “Kurds”, here as fellow brigands. mujtamiʿa, “gathered”, is feminine singular agreeing with a broken plural. ḥaram, “sacred precinct, sanctuary”. atā bi-, “to come with”, i.e. to bring. The tale of woe ends in rhyme: rijālī, amwālī, ḥālī, “my men, my goods, my plight”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ التَّاجِرَ بَكَى بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْمَلِكِ رُومْزَانَ وَحَوْقَلَ وَاشْتَكَى فَرَحِمَهُ الْمَلِكُ وَرَقَّ إِلَيْهِ وَكَذَلِكَ رَحِمَهُ ابْنُ أَخِيهِ الْمَلِكُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-tājira bakā bayna yadayi al-maliki Rūmzāna wa-ḥawqala wa-ishtakā fa-raḥimahu al-maliku wa-raqqa ilayhi wa-kadhālika raḥimahu ibnu akhīhi al-maliku Kāna Mā Kāna
sentences.l: Then the merchant wept between the two hands of King Rūmzān, and said-the-ḥawqala and complained; and the king pitied him and softened toward him; and likewise his brother's son, King Kān Mā Kān, pitied him.
sentences.i: Then the merchant wept before King Rūmzān, crying that there is no power and no strength save in God, and poured out his complaint. The king took pity on him and was moved for him, and so too was his nephew, King Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, i.e. in the presence of. ḥawqala is a verb coined from the formula lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāh, “there is no might and no power except in God”, the cry of a man in distress. raqqa ilā (more usually raqqa li-), “to feel tender toward”.

sentences.t: وَحَلَفُوا أَنَّهُمْ يَخْرُجُونَ إِلَيْهِمْ فَخَرَجُوا إِلَيْهِمْ فِي مِائَةِ فَارِسٍ كُلُّ فَارِسٍ مِنْهُمْ يُعَدُّ بَيْنَ الرِّجَالِ بِأُلُوفٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥalafū annahum yakhrujūna ilayhim fa-kharajū ilayhim fī miʾati fārisin kullu fārisin minhum yuʿaddu bayna al-rijāli bi-ulūfin
sentences.l: And they swore that they would go-out against them; and they went-out against them with a hundred horsemen, every horseman of them counted among the men as thousands.
sentences.i: They swore to ride out against the robbers, and so they did, with a hundred horsemen, every one of whom was reckoned among men as worth thousands.
sentences.n: kharaja ilā, “to go out to (meet)”, here “to sally against”. fī miʾati fārisin, “in a hundred horsemen”: fī marks the company one rides with. The shadda on يعدّ is the print's; yuʿaddu bi-ulūfin, “is counted for thousands”, a stock praise of a champion.

sentences.t: وَذَلِكَ التَّاجِرُ سَارَ أَمَامَهُمْ يَدُلُّهُمْ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika al-tājiru sāra amāmahum yadulluhum ʿalā al-ṭarīqi
sentences.l: And that merchant went before them, guiding-them on the road.
sentences.i: The merchant rode ahead of them, showing them the way.
sentences.n: dalla ʿalā, “to show the way to, guide”; the shadda on يدلّهم is the print's.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا سَائِرِينَ ذَلِكَ النَّهَارَ وَطُولَ اللَّيْلِ إِلَى السَّحَرِ حَتَّى أَشْرَفُوا عَلَى وَادٍ غَزِيرِ الْأَنْهَارِ كَثِيرِ الْأَشْجَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū sāʾirīna dhālika al-nahāra wa-ṭūla al-layli ilā al-saḥari ḥattā ashrafū ʿalā wādin ghazīri al-anhāri kathīri al-ashjāri
sentences.l: And they did not cease journeying that day and the length of the night until the dawn-twilight, until they looked-down upon a valley abundant of streams, plentiful of trees.
sentences.i: They rode on all that day and the whole night through until just before dawn, when they came out above a valley rich in streams and thick with trees.
sentences.n: saḥar, the last part of the night before dawn. ashrafa ʿalā, “to look down on from a height”, to come in sight of. The valley is in rhyme, ghazīr al-anhār, kathīr al-ashjār, “abundant of rivers, plentiful of trees”: each adjective is in construct with what it has much of.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدُوا الْقَوْمَ قَدْ تَفَرَّقُوا فِي ذَلِكَ الْوَادِي وَقَسَمُوا بَيْنَهُمْ أَحْمَالَ ذَلِكَ التَّاجِرِ وَبَقِيَ الْبَعْضُ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadū al-qawma qad tafarraqū fī dhālika al-wādī wa-qasamū baynahum aḥmāla dhālika al-tājiri wa-baqiya al-baʿḍu
sentences.l: And they found the people had dispersed in that valley, and divided among them the loads of that merchant, and the some remained.
sentences.i: There they found the robbers scattered through the valley; they had shared out the merchant's loads among themselves, though some still remained.
sentences.n: wa-baqiya al-baʿḍu, “and the part remained”, is terse: most likely that part of the goods was still undivided, which the recovery of the merchant's property below bears out; it could also mean that some of the band had stayed together. al-qawm, “the people”, here “the band”.

sentences.t: فَأَطْبَقَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْمِائَةُ فَارِسٍ وَأَحَاطُوا بِهِمْ مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَصَاحَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ هُوَ وَابْنُ أَخِيهِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭbaqa ʿalayhimu al-miʾatu fārisin wa-aḥāṭū bihim min kulli makānin wa-ṣāḥa ʿalayhimu al-maliku Rūmzānu huwa wa-ibnu akhīhi Kāna Mā Kāna
sentences.l: And the hundred horsemen closed-in upon them, and surrounded them from every place, and King Rūmzān shouted at them, he and his brother's son Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: The hundred horsemen closed in on them and surrounded them on every side, and King Rūmzān and his nephew Kān Mā Kān raised the war cry against them.
sentences.n: aṭbaqa ʿalā, “to close over, fall upon from all sides”. al-miʾatu fārisin, “the hundred horseman”: the article goes on the numeral and the counted noun stays singular genitive, a common post-classical construction. ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to shout against”, to charge with a cry. The verb is singular before its compound subject, “King Rūmzān, he and his nephew”.

sentences.t: فَمَا كَانَ غَيْرُ سَاعَةٍ حَتَّي أَسَرُوا الْجَمِيعَ وَكَانُوا نَحْوَ ثَلٰثِمِائَةِ فَارِسٍ مُجْتَمِعِينَ مِنْ أَوْبَاشِ الْعُرْبَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā kāna ghayru sāʿatin ḥattā asarū al-jamīʿa wa-kānū naḥwa thalāthimiʾati fārisin mujtamiʿīna min awbāshi al-ʿurbāni
sentences.l: And there was not other-than an hour until they captured all; and they were about three-hundred horsemen gathered from the riff-raff of the Bedouins.
sentences.i: It was no more than an hour before they had taken them all prisoner. There were some three hundred horsemen, gathered from the rabble of the desert Arabs.
sentences.n: fa-mā kāna ghayru sāʿatin ḥattā, “there was not but an hour before”, a stock phrase for speed. ḥattā is spelt with ي here. The print writes thalāth, “three”, defectively, without the long ā (ثلثمائة); the dagger alif is the print's. awbāsh, “riff-raff, rabble”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَسَرُوهُمْ أَخَذُوا مَا مَعَهُمْ مِنْ مَالِ التَّاجِرِ وَشَدُّوا وَثَاقَهُمْ وَطَلَعُوا بِهِمْ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā asarūhum akhadhū mā maʿahum min māli al-tājiri wa-shaddū wathāqahum wa-ṭalaʿū bihim ilā madīnati Baghdāda
sentences.l: And when they captured them, they took what (was) with them of the merchant's goods, and tightened their bonds, and went-up with them to the city of Baghdad.
sentences.i: Having captured them, they took back what the band had of the merchant's goods, bound them fast, and brought them up to the city of Baghdad.
sentences.n: shadda al-wathāqa, “to tighten the bond”, the Qurʾānic phrase for binding captives. ṭalaʿa bi-, “to go up with”, i.e. to bring up: colloquial, and used of going to the capital.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ جَلَسَ الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ هُوَ وَابْنُ أَخِيهِ الْمَلِكُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ عَلَى تَخْتٍ وَاحِدٍ مَعَ بَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika jalasa al-maliku Rūmzānu huwa wa-ibnu akhīhi al-maliku Kāna Mā Kāna ʿalā takhtin wāḥidin maʿa baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: And at that King Rūmzān sat, he and his brother's son King Kān Mā Kān, on one throne together.
sentences.i: Then King Rūmzān and his nephew King Kān Mā Kān sat down together on a single throne.
sentences.n: takht, “throne”, a Persian word. maʿa baʿḍihimā, “with each other”, colloquial for “together”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ عَرَضُوا الْجَمِيعَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمَا وَسَأَلَاهُمْ عَنْ حَالِهِمْ وَعَنْ كِبَارِهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma ʿaraḍū al-jamīʿa bayna aydīhimā wa-saʾalāhum ʿan ḥālihim wa-ʿan kibārihim
sentences.l: Then they paraded all of them between the hands of the two, and the two asked them about their state and about their great-ones.
sentences.i: Then all the prisoners were paraded before the two kings, who questioned them about themselves and about their leaders.
sentences.n: ʿaraḍa, “to present, parade (before a ruler)”; the plural subject is the soldiers, unnamed. saʾalāhum is dual: the two kings ask. kibār, “the great ones”, the chiefs.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا مَا لَنَا كِبَارٌ غَيْرُ ثَلٰثَةِ أَشْخَاصٍ وَهُمُ الَّذِينَ جَمَعُونَا مِنْ سَائِرِ النَّوَاحِي وَالْأَقْطَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū mā lanā kibārun ghayru thalāthati ashkhāṣin wa-humu alladhīna jamaʿūnā min sāʾiri al-nawāḥī wa-al-aqṭāri
sentences.l: And they said: There are not to us great-ones other-than three persons, and they (are) the ones who gathered-us from all the districts and the regions.
sentences.i: They answered, “We have no leaders but three men, and it was they who gathered us together from every quarter and region.”
sentences.n: mā lanā, “we have not”. shakhṣ, “person, individual”. sāʾir, “all, the whole of” (in Classical usage more strictly “the rest of”).

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لَهُمْ مَيِّزُوهُمْ لَنَا بِأَعْيَانِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā lahum mayyizūhum lanā bi-aʿyānihim
sentences.l: And the two said to them: Pick-them-out for us by their very-selves.
sentences.i: The two kings said to them, “Point them out to us, each one by name and face.”
sentences.n: mayyaza, “to distinguish, single out”; the shadda on ميّزوهم is the print's. bi-aʿyānihim, “by their very selves”, ʿayn being “eye” and also “the thing itself”: “individually, in person”.

sentences.t: فَمَيَّزُوهُمْ لَهُمَا فَأَمَرَا بِالْقَبْضِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَإِطْلَاقِ بَقِيَّةِ أَصْحَابِهِمْ بَعْدَ أَخْذِ جَمِيعِ مَا مَعَهُمْ مِنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَتَسْلِيمِهِ لِلتَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-mayyazūhum lahumā fa-amarā bi-al-qabḍi ʿalayhim wa-iṭlāqi baqiyyati aṣḥābihim baʿda akhdhi jamīʿi mā maʿahum mina al-amwāli wa-taslīmihi li-al-tājiri
sentences.l: So they picked-them-out for the two of them; and the two commanded the seizing of them, and the releasing of the rest of their companions, after the taking of all that was with them of the wealth and the handing of it over to the merchant.
sentences.i: So they pointed the three out to the two kings, who ordered them to be seized and the rest of their followers set free, once everything they had on them of the plunder had been taken and handed over to the merchant.
sentences.n: The bandits point out their three chiefs, as the kings had asked. amarā bi-, “the two commanded”: the verb takes what is ordered with bi-. The dual is the two kings, Rūmzān and Kān Mā Kān; taslīmihi, “handing it over”, takes a masculine “it” for mā, “all that”.

sentences.t: فَتَفَقَّدَ التَّاجِرُ قُمَاشَهُ وَمَا لَهُ فَوَجَدَهُ قَدْ هَلَكَ رُبْعُهُ فَوَعَدُوهُ أَنَّهُمْ يُعَوِّضُونَ لَهُ جَمِيعَ مَاضَاعَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-tafaqqada al-tājiru qumāshahu wa-mā lahu fa-wajadahu qad halaka rubʿuhu fa-waʿadūhu annahum yuʿawwiḍūna lahu jamīʿa mā ḍāʿa minhu
sentences.l: And the merchant went-over his stuffs and what was his, and found it: a quarter of it had perished; and they promised him that they would make-good to him all that had been-lost from him.
sentences.i: The merchant looked over his bales and his belongings and found that a quarter of them were gone; and they promised to make good to him everything he had lost.
sentences.n: tafaqqada, “to inspect, look over (what one has, to see what is missing)”. qumāsh, “cloth, stuffs”, a merchant's goods. wa-mā lahu, “and what was his”; it could also be taken as the single word mālahu, “his property”, with the same sense. ʿawwaḍa, “to make good, compensate”, takes the injured man here with li- (lahu) rather than as a direct object, a colloquial turn. The print runs mā ḍāʿa, “what was lost”, together as one word, ماضاع.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَخْرَجَ التَّاجِرُ كِتَابَيْنِ أَحَدُهُمَا بِخَطِّ شَرْكَانَ وَالْآخَرُ بِخَطِّ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika akhraja al-tājiru kitābayni aḥaduhumā bi-khaṭṭi Sharrukāna wa-al-ākharu bi-khaṭṭi Nuzhati al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And at that the merchant brought-out two letters, one of them in the hand of Sharrukān and the other in the hand of Nuzhat al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then the merchant brought out two letters, one in Sharrukān's handwriting and the other in Nuzhat al-Zamān's.
sentences.n: kitāb, here “letter, written document” rather than “book”. bi-khaṭṭi, “in the hand(writing) of”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ كَانَ هَذَا التَّاجِرُ اشْتَرَى نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ مِنَ الْبَدَوِيِّ وَهِيَ بِكْرٌ وَقَدَّمَهَا لِأَخِيهَا شَرْكَانَ وَجَرَى بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ أَخِيهَا مَاجَرَى
sentences.tr: wa-qad kāna hādhā al-tājiru ishtarā Nuzhata al-Zamāni mina al-badawiyyi wa-hiya bikrun wa-qaddamahā li-akhīhā Sharrukāna wa-jarā baynahā wa-bayna akhīhā mā jarā
sentences.l: And this merchant had bought Nuzhat al-Zamān from the Bedouin while she was a virgin, and presented her to her brother Sharrukān; and there happened between her and her brother what happened.
sentences.i: For this was the very merchant who had bought Nuzhat al-Zamān, still a virgin, from the Bedouin and presented her to her brother Sharrukān; and between her and her brother there passed what passed.
sentences.n: kāna … ishtarā, “had bought”: kāna with a perfect gives the pluperfect. The narrator reminds us of the earlier tale: neither knowing the other, Sharrukān married his sister and she bore him a daughter; “what passed” is the text's own veiled phrase. The print runs mā jarā, “what happened”, together as one word, ماجرى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَفَ عَلَى الْكِتَابَيْنِ وَعَرَفَ خَطَّ عَمِّهِ شَرْكَانَ وَسَمِعَ حِكَايَةَ عَمَّتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika Kāna Mā Kāna waqafa ʿalā al-kitābayni wa-ʿarafa khaṭṭa ʿammihi Sharrukāna wa-samiʿa ḥikāyata ʿammatihi Nuzhati al-Zamāni
sentences.l: Then King Kān Mā Kān came-upon the two letters, and knew the hand of his uncle Sharrukān, and heard the story of his aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then King Kān Mā Kān read the two letters, recognised the hand of his uncle Sharrukān, and heard the story of his aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān.
sentences.n: waqafa ʿalā, literally “to stand upon”, is the regular phrase for reading or examining a document. Sharrukān is indeed his paternal uncle (ʿamm), brother of his father Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and Nuzhat al-Zamān his paternal aunt (ʿamma).

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا بِذَلِكَ الْكِتَابِ الثَّانِي الَّذِي كَانَتْ كَتَبَتْهُ لِلتَّاجِرِ الَّذِي ضَاعَ مِنْهَا الْمَالُ وَأَخْبَرَهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ بِقِصَّةِ التَّاجِرِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا إِلَى آخِرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala ʿalayhā bi-dhālika al-kitābi al-thānī alladhī kānat katabathu li-al-tājiri alladhī ḍāʿa minhā al-mālu wa-akhbarahā Kāna Mā Kāna bi-qiṣṣati al-tājiri min awwalihā ilā ākhirihā
sentences.l: So he went-in to her with that second letter which she had written for the merchant, the-one-from-whom (fem.) the wealth was lost; and Kān Mā Kān told her the tale of the merchant from its beginning to its end.
sentences.i: So he went in to her with the second letter, the one she had once written for the merchant, the man who had now been robbed; and Kān Mā Kān told her the merchant's story from beginning to end.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone in their rooms)”; bi-, “bringing”. alladhī ḍāʿa minhā al-māl is doubtful as printed: alladhī should refer to the merchant, but minhā, “from her / from it (f.)”, is feminine. Most likely minhu, “from him”, is meant (“the merchant whose goods were lost”); minhā might otherwise refer back to the qāfila, the caravan, or loosely to the goods. The print is kept and rendered as it stands. In the second clause the name Kān Mā Kān is repeated as subject, and is taken here as indeclinable, as always.

sentences.t: فَعَرَفَتْهُ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ وَعَرَفَتْ خَطَّهَا وَأَخْرَجَتْ لِلتَّاجِرِ الضِّيَافَاتِ وَوَصَّتْ عَلَيْهِ أَخَاهَا الْمَلِكَ رُومْزَانَ وَابْنَ أَخِيهَا الْمَلِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَأَمَرَ لَهُ بِأَمْوَالٍ وَعَبِيدٍ وَغِلْمَانٍ مِنْ أَجْلِ خِدْمَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿarafathu Nuzhatu al-Zamāni wa-ʿarafat khaṭṭahā wa-akhrajat li-al-tājiri al-ḍiyāfāti wa-waṣṣat ʿalayhi akhāhā al-malika Rūmzāna wa-ibna akhīhā al-malika Kāna Mā Kāna fa-amara lahu bi-amwālin wa-ʿabīdin wa-ghilmānin min ajli khidmatihi
sentences.l: And Nuzhat al-Zamān knew it, and knew her (own) hand; and she brought-out for the merchant the hospitalities, and charged concerning-him her brother King Rūmzān and her brother's son King Kān Mā Kān; and he ordered for him wealth and slaves and pages for the sake of his service.
sentences.i: Nuzhat al-Zamān recognised the letter and her own handwriting. She had the merchant lavishly entertained and commended him to the care of her brother King Rūmzān and her nephew King Kān Mā Kān; and he ordered him gifts of money, with slaves and pages to wait on him.
sentences.n: akhrajat al-ḍiyāfāt, “she brought out the hospitalities”, i.e. ordered feasts and gifts of welcome; ḍiyāfa is the entertainment given a guest. waṣṣā X ʿalā Y, “to charge X concerning Y, commend Y to X's care”: waṣṣat is the Classical feminine of waṣṣā. fa-amara, “and he ordered”, is singular though two kings have just been named; either each king in turn or Rūmzān, the first named, is meant. amara lahu bi-, “to order (something) for someone”.

sentences.t: وَأَرْسَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ مِائَةَ أَلْفِ دِرْهَمٍ مِنَ الْمَالِ وَخَمْسِينَ حِمْلًا مِنَ الْبَضَائِعِ وَقَدْأَ تْحَفَتْهُ بِهَدَايَا
sentences.tr: wa-arsalat ilayhi Nuzhatu al-Zamāni miʾata alfi dirhamin mina al-māli wa-khamsīna ḥimlan mina al-baḍāʾiʿi wa-qad atḥafathu bi-hadāyā
sentences.l: And Nuzhat al-Zamān sent to him a hundred thousand dirhams of money, and fifty loads of merchandise, and had-already favoured-him with gifts.
sentences.i: And Nuzhat al-Zamān sent him a hundred thousand dirhams in money and fifty loads of merchandise, and showered him with presents besides.
sentences.n: The print splits qad atḥafathu, “she had favoured him”, after the alif of the verb, as وقدا تحفته; the spacing is kept and the words are pointed across the split. atḥafa bi-, “to present (someone) with a rare gift (tuḥfa)”. ḥiml, a camel- or mule-load. hadāyā, “gifts”, is a diptote and so takes no nunation after bi-.

sentences.t: وَأَرْسَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ تَطْلُبُهُ فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ طَلَعَتْ لَهُ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَأَعْلَمَتْهُ أَنَّهَا بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَأَنَّ أَخَاهَا الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ وَأَنَّ ابْنَ أَخِيهَا الْمَلِكُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-arsalat ilayhi taṭlubuhu fa-lammā ḥaḍara ṭalaʿat lahu wa-sallamat ʿalayhi wa-aʿlamathu annahā bintu al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni wa-anna akhāhā al-maliku Rūmzānu wa-anna ibna akhīhā al-maliku Kāna Mā Kāna
sentences.l: And she sent to him, summoning him; and when he came, she came-out to him and greeted him, and let-him-know that she was the daughter of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and that her brother was King Rūmzān, and that her brother's son was King Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: Then she sent for him, and when he came she came out to meet him, greeted him, and told him that she was the daughter of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, that her brother was King Rūmzān, and that her nephew was King Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: arsalat ilayhi taṭlubuhu, “she sent to him, asking for him”: the imperfect describes the purpose of the sending. ṭalaʿat lahu, “she came out to him”, colloquial ṭalaʿa, “to come up, come out”: she shows herself to him in person. anna akhāhā al-maliku Rūmzānu: after anna the subject is accusative (akhāhā) and the predicate nominative (al-maliku).

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ التَّاجِرُ بِذَلِكَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَهَنَّأَهَا بِسَلَامَتِهَا وَاجْتِمَاعِهَا بِأَخِيهَا وَقَبَّلَ يَدَيْهَا وَشَكَرَهَا عَلَى فِعْلِهَا وَقَالَ لَهَا وَاللَّهِ مَا ضَاعَ الْجَمِيلُ مَعَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-tājiru bi-dhālika faraḥan shadīdan wa-hannaʾahā bi-salāmatihā wa-ijtimāʿihā bi-akhīhā wa-qabbala yadayhā wa-shakarahā ʿalā fiʿlihā wa-qāla lahā wa-Allāhi mā ḍāʿa al-jamīlu maʿaki
sentences.l: And the merchant rejoiced at that with an intense rejoicing, and congratulated her on her safety and her being-united with her brother, and kissed her hands and thanked her for her deed, and said to her: By God, the kindness was not lost with you!
sentences.i: The merchant was overjoyed at this. He wished her joy of her safety and of her reunion with her brother, kissed her hands, and thanked her for what she had done, saying, “By God, the kindness I once showed you was not wasted!”
sentences.n: faraḥan shadīdan, “with intense joy”, an internal (cognate) accusative. hannaʾa bi-, “to congratulate on”. ijtimāʿ bi-, “meeting with, being reunited with”. mā ḍāʿa al-jamīlu maʿaki, “the good deed was not lost with you”: a proverbial phrase, “kindness done to you has been repaid”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَخَلَتْ إِلَى خِدْرِهَا وَأَقَامَ التَّاجِرُ عِنْدَهُمْ ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ وَدَّعَهُمْ وَرَحَلَ إِلَى بِلَادِ الشَّامِ
sentences.tr: thumma dakhalat ilā khidrihā wa-aqāma al-tājiru ʿindahum thalāthata ayyāmin thumma waddaʿahum wa-raḥala ilā bilādi al-Shāmi
sentences.l: Then she went-in to her curtained-chamber; and the merchant stayed with them three days, then bade-them-farewell and journeyed to the lands of Syria.
sentences.i: Then she withdrew to her private apartments. The merchant stayed with them three days; then he took his leave of them and set out for the land of Syria.
sentences.n: khidr, the curtained part of a house reserved to the women. thalāthata, written defectively ثلٰثة in the print, with the long ā as a small dagger alif. al-Shām, Greater Syria; bilād al-Shām, “the lands of Syria”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَحْضَرَ الْمُلُوكُ الثَّلٰثَةَ أَشْخَاصِ اللُّصُوصِ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا رُؤَسَاءَ قُطَّاعِ الطَّرِيقِ وَسَأَلُوهُمْ عَنْ حَالِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aḥḍara al-mulūku al-thalāthata ashkhāṣi al-luṣūṣi alladhīna kānū ruʾasāʾa quṭṭāʿi al-ṭarīqi wa-saʾalūhum ʿan ḥālihim
sentences.l: And after that the kings had-brought the three persons of the thieves who were the heads of the cutters of the road, and asked them about their case.
sentences.i: After this the kings had the three robbers brought before them, the ringleaders of the highwaymen, and questioned them about themselves.
sentences.n: al-thalāthata ashkhāṣi, “the three persons”: Middle Arabic puts the article on the numeral and lets the counted noun follow (Classical al-ashkhāṣa al-thalāthata); ashkhāṣ is pointed here in construct with al-luṣūṣ, “the thieves”. al-mulūk, “the kings”, is plural for the two kings; the verb aḥḍara stands in the singular before its subject, as Classical allows, and saʾalūhum then follows in the plural. quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq, “cutters of the road”, the ordinary term for highwaymen.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ وَقَالَ اعْلَمُوا أَنِّي رَجُلٌ بَدَوِيٌّ أَقِفُ فِى الطَّرِيقِ لِأَخْطَفَ الصِّغَارَ وَالْبَنَاتِ الْأَبْكَارَ وَأَبِيعَهُمْ لِلتُّجَّارِ وَدُمْتُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ مُدَّةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ إِلَى هَذِهِ الْأَيَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama wāḥidun minhum wa-qāla iʿlamū annī rajulun badawiyyun aqifu fī al-ṭarīqi li-akhṭafa al-ṣighāra wa-al-banāti al-abkāra wa-abīʿahum li-al-tujjāri wa-dumtu ʿalā dhālika muddatan mina al-zamāni ilā hādhihi al-ayyāmi
sentences.l: And one of them came-forward and said: Know that I am a Bedouin man; I stand in the road to snatch the young-ones and the girls, the virgin-ones, and sell them to the merchants; and I continued in that a span of time, up to these days.
sentences.i: One of them came forward and said, “Know that I am a Bedouin. I used to lie in wait on the road to snatch little children and maiden girls and sell them to the merchants, and I kept at it for a long while, down to these present days.
sentences.n: The speech falls into loose rhyme: al-abkār, “the virgins”, with al-tujjār, “the merchants”, and al-zamān with al-ayyām. li-akhṭafa … wa-abīʿahum, subjunctive after li-, “in order to”. al-ṣighār, “the little ones”, here children. dumtu ʿalā, “I persisted in”.

sentences.t: وَأَغْرَانِي الشَّيْطَانُ فَاتَّفَقْتُ مَعَ هَذَيْنِ الشَّقِيَّيْنِ عَلَى جَمْعِ الْأَوْبَاشِ مِنَ الْأَعْرَابِ وَالْبُلْدَانِ لِأَجْلِ نَهْبِ الْأَمْوَالِ وَقَطْعِ الطَّرِيقِ عَلَى التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-aghrānī al-shayṭānu fa-ittafaqtu maʿa hādhayni al-shaqiyyayni ʿalā jamʿi al-awbāshi mina al-aʿrābi wa-al-buldāni li-ajli nahbi al-amwāli wa-qaṭʿi al-ṭarīqi ʿalā al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And the Devil tempted-me, and I agreed with these two wretched-ones on the gathering of the rabble from the Bedouins and the towns, for the sake of the plundering of wealth and the cutting of the road against the merchants.
sentences.i: Then the Devil led me on, and I joined with these two wretches in gathering riff-raff from the desert tribes and the towns, to plunder goods and waylay the merchants on the road.”
sentences.n: aghrā, “to egg on, tempt”. shaqī, “wretched, damned”, in the dual; the shadda on الشقيّين is the print's. al-aʿrāb, “the Bedouin, desert Arabs”, set against al-buldān, “the towns, settled lands”. qaṭaʿa al-ṭarīqa ʿalā, “to cut the road against”, i.e. to waylay.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَهُ احْكِ لَنَا عَلَى أَعْجَبِ مَا رَأَيْتَ فِي خَطْفِكَ الصِّغَارَ وَالْبَنَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lahu iḥki lanā ʿalā aʿjabi mā raʾayta fī khaṭfika al-ṣighāra wa-al-banāti
sentences.l: And they said to him: Tell us about the most-wondrous of what you saw in your snatching of the young-ones and the girls.
sentences.i: They said to him, “Tell us the strangest thing you ever met with in your stealing of children and girls.”
sentences.n: ḥakā ʿalā, “to tell about”: colloquial, where Classical says ḥakā ʿan. khaṭfika al-ṣighāra, “your snatching the children”: the verbal noun governs its object in the accusative, as the verb would.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمْ أَعْجَبُ مَا جَرَى لِي يَا مُلُوكَ الزَّمَانِ أَنَّنِي مِنْ مُدَّةِ اثْنَتَيْنِ وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً خَطَفْتُ بِنْتًا مِنْ بَنَاتِ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahum aʿjabu mā jarā lī yā mulūka al-zamāni annanī min muddati ithnatayni wa-ʿishrīna sanatan khaṭaftu bintan min banāti Bayti al-Maqdisi dhāta yawmin mina al-ayyāmi
sentences.l: And he said to them: The most-wondrous of what befell me, O kings of the age, is that I, from a span of two-and-twenty years, snatched a girl of the girls of the House of the Holy-place, one day of the days.
sentences.i: He said to them, “The strangest thing that ever befell me, O kings of the age, was this: twenty-two years ago, one day, I carried off a girl from Jerusalem.
sentences.n: min muddati … sanatan, “from a span of … years”, i.e. “… years ago”. Bayt al-Maqdis, “the House of the Holy Place”, is Jerusalem. dhāta yawmin mina al-ayyāmi, “one day of the days”, a stock storyteller's phrase.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الْبِنْتُ ذَاتَ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ غَيْرَ أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ خَدَّامَةً وَعَلَيْهَا أَثْوَابٌ خَلِقَةٌ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهَا قِطْعَةُ عَبَاءَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tilka al-bintu dhāta ḥusnin wa-jamālin ghayra annahā kānat khaddāmatan wa-ʿalayhā athwābun khaliqatun wa-ʿalā raʾsihā qiṭʿatu ʿabāʾatin
sentences.l: And that girl was possessed-of beauty and loveliness, except that she was a serving-woman, and on her were garments worn-out, and on her head a piece of a cloak.
sentences.i: That girl was lovely and fair of face, but she was a serving-woman, dressed in threadbare clothes, with a scrap of a cloak over her head.
sentences.n: The print has إثواب, a misprint for اثواب, corrected here: the hamza is set below the alif, where athwāb, “garments”, needs it above. khaddāma, “serving-woman, drudge”, an intensive form. khaliqa, “worn-out, threadbare”, agrees in the feminine singular with the non-human plural athwāb. ʿabāʾa, the loose woollen cloak of the desert.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُهَا قَدْ خَرَجَتْ مِنَ الْخَانِ فَخَطَفْتُهَا بِحِيلَةٍ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ وَحَمَلْتُهَا عَلَى جَمَلٍ وَسَبَقْتُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytuhā qad kharajat mina al-khāni fa-khaṭaftuhā bi-ḥīlatin fī tilka al-sāʿati wa-ḥamaltuhā ʿalā jamalin wa-sabaqtu bihā
sentences.l: And I saw her, she having come-out from the inn; so I snatched her by a ruse in that hour, and carried her on a camel, and raced-ahead with her.
sentences.i: I saw her come out of the inn, and there and then I seized her by a trick, set her on a camel, and made off with her.
sentences.n: khān, an inn or caravanserai. sabaqa bi-, “to outrun (others) with”, i.e. to get clean away with her before pursuit.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي أَصْلِي أَنَّنِي أَذْهَبُ بِهَا إِلَى أَهْلِي فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَأَجْعَلُهَا عِنْدِي تَرْعَى الْجِمَالَ وَتَجْمَعُ الْبَعْرَ مِنَ الْوَادِي
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī aṣlī annanī adhhabu bihā ilā ahlī fī al-barriyyati wa-ajʿaluhā ʿindī tarʿā al-jimāla wa-tajmaʿu al-baʿra mina al-wādī
sentences.l: And it was in my root(-intention) that I would go with her to my people in the open-desert, and set her with me herding the camels and gathering the dung from the valley.
sentences.i: My plan was to take her to my people in the desert and keep her with me to herd the camels and gather dung in the valley.
sentences.n: fī aṣlī, “in my root”, i.e. “my original intention”, an idiomatic use. adhhabu bi-, “to go with, take away”. baʿr, the dried droppings of camels, gathered as fuel; wādī, a dry valley or watercourse.

sentences.t: فَبَكَتْ بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا فَدَنَوْتُ مِنْهَا وَضَرَبْتُهَا ضَرْبًا وَجِيعًا وَأَخَذْتُهَا وَسِرْتُ بِهَا إِلَى مَدِينَةِ دِمَشْقَ
sentences.tr: fa-bakat bukāʾan shadīdan fa-danawtu minhā wa-ḍarabtuhā ḍarban wajīʿan wa-akhadhtuhā wa-sirtu bihā ilā madīnati Dimashqa
sentences.l: And she wept a weeping intense; and I drew-near to her and beat her a beating painful, and took her and journeyed with her to the city of Damascus.
sentences.i: She wept bitterly, so I went up to her and gave her a cruel beating; then I took her and travelled with her to the city of Damascus.
sentences.n: bakat bukāʾan shadīdan, ḍarabtuhā ḍarban wajīʿan: each verb is followed by its own verbal noun with an adjective (the cognate accusative), the usual way of saying “wept bitterly”, “beat cruelly”. “She” is the girl the Bedouin snatched from the khan in Jerusalem.

sentences.t: فَرَآهَا مَعِي تَاجِرٌ فَتَحَيَّرَ عَقْلُهُ لَمَّا رَآهَا وَأَعْجَبَتْهُ فَصَاحَتُهَا وَأَرَادَ اشْتِرَاؤُهَا مِنِّي وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَزِيدُنِي فِي ثَمَنِهَا حَتَّى بِعْتُهَا لَهُ بِمِائَةِ أَلْفِ دِرْهَمٍ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾāhā maʿī tājirun fa-taḥayyara ʿaqluhu lammā raʾāhā wa-aʿjabathu faṣāḥatuhā wa-arāda ishtirāʾuhā minnī wa-lam yazal yazīdunī fī thamanihā ḥattā biʿtuhā lahu bi-miʾati alfi dirhamin
sentences.l: And a merchant saw her with me, and his mind was bewildered when he saw her, and her eloquence pleased him; and he wanted the buying-of-her from me, and did not cease increasing-to-me in her price until I sold her to him for a hundred thousand dirhams.
sentences.i: A merchant saw her with me and was dazzled at the sight of her, and her eloquence charmed him. He wished to buy her from me, and kept raising his offer until I sold her to him for a hundred thousand dirhams.
sentences.n: The print writes اشتراؤها with the hamza on wāw, the spelling of a nominative ishtirāʾuhā, though as the object of arāda Classical Arabic wants the accusative ishtirāʾahā (اشتراءها); the print's form is kept and pointed as it stands. yazīdunī fī thamanihā, “he kept increasing to me in her price”: kept raising his bid.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ مَا أَعْطَيْتُهَا لَهُ رَأَيْتُ مِنْهَا فَصَاحَةً عَظِيمَةً وَبَلَغَنِي أَنَّ التَّاجِرَ كَسَاهَا كِسْوَةً مَلِيحَةً وَقَدَّمَهَا إِلَى الْمَلِكِ صَاحِبِ دِمَشْقَ فَأَعْطَاهُ قَدْرَ الْمَبْلَغِ الَّذِي دَفَعَهُ إِلَيَّ مَرَّتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda mā aʿṭaytuhā lahu raʾaytu minhā faṣāḥatan ʿaẓīmatan wa-balaghanī anna al-tājira kasāhā kiswatan malīḥatan wa-qaddamahā ilā al-maliki ṣāḥibi Dimashqa fa-aʿṭāhu qadra al-mablaghi alladhī dafaʿahu ilayya marratayni
sentences.l: And at-the-time-when I gave her to him, I saw from her a great eloquence; and it reached me that the merchant clothed her in a fine clothing and presented her to the king, lord of Damascus, and he gave him the measure of the sum which he had paid to me twice-over.
sentences.i: As I handed her over to him I saw how wonderfully eloquent she was; and I heard afterwards that the merchant dressed her in fine clothes and presented her to the king who ruled Damascus, and the king gave him twice the sum he had paid me.
sentences.n: ʿinda mā, “at the moment when”, set as two words. ṣāḥib Dimashq, “the lord of Damascus”: Sharrukān, who then governed it for his father. qadra al-mablaghi … marratayni, “the amount of the sum … twice”: double the price. The shadda on اليّ (ilayya, “to me”) is the print's.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا يَا مُلُوكَ الزَّمَانِ أَعْجَبُ مَاجَرَى لِي وَلَعَمْرِي إِنَّ ذَلِكَ الثَّمَنَ قَلِيلٌ فِي تِلْكَ الْبِنْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā yā mulūka al-zamāni aʿjabu mā jarā lī wa-la-ʿamrī inna dhālika al-thamana qalīlun fī tilka al-binti
sentences.l: And this, O kings of the time, is the most-wondrous of what befell me; and by-my-life, that price is little for that girl.
sentences.i: And this, O kings of the age, is the strangest thing that ever befell me; and by my life, that price was too little for such a girl.”
sentences.n: The print runs mā jarā, “what happened”, together as ماجرى, as it does throughout. la-ʿamrī, “by my life”, an oath, followed by inna. qalīl fī, “little for”: too low a price for.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمُلُوكُ هَذِهِ الْحِكَايَةَ تَعَجَّبُوا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-mulūku hādhihi al-ḥikāyata taʿajjabū
sentences.l: And when the kings heard this tale, they wondered.
sentences.i: When the kings heard this story they marvelled.
sentences.n: samiʿa al-mulūku, “the kings heard”: a verb standing before its plural subject stays singular; the verb after it, taʿajjabū, is plural.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ مِنَ الْبَدَوِيِّ مَاحَكَاهُ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهَا ظَلَامًا وَصَاحَتْ وَقَالَتْ لِأَخِيهَا رُومْزَانَ إِنَّ هَذَا الْبَدَوِيَّ الَّذِي كَانَ خَطَفَنِي مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ بِعَيْنِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ شَكٍّ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā samiʿat Nuzhatu al-Zamāni mina al-badawiyyi mā ḥakāhu ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihā ẓalāman wa-ṣāḥat wa-qālat li-akhīhā Rūmzāna inna hādhā al-badawiyya alladhī kāna khaṭafanī min Bayti al-Maqdisi bi-ʿaynihi min ghayri shakkin
sentences.l: And when Nuzhat al-Zamān heard from the Bedouin what he related, the light in her face became darkness, and she cried-out and said to her brother Rūmzān: This Bedouin is the-one who had snatched me from the House of the Holy-place, his very-self, without doubt!
sentences.i: But when Nuzhat al-Zamān heard the Bedouin's tale, the light in her face turned to darkness, and she cried out and said to her brother Rūmzān, “This Bedouin is the very man who carried me off from Jerusalem, beyond all doubt!”
sentences.n: The print runs mā ḥakāhu, “what he told”, together as ماحكاه. inna hādhā al-badawiyya alladhī …, “this Bedouin (is) the one who …”, with no copula; bi-ʿaynihi, “in his very self”, makes it emphatic. kāna khaṭafanī, kāna with a perfect, a pluperfect: “had snatched me”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ حَكَتْ لَهُمْ جَمِيعَ مَاجَرَى لَهَا مَعَهُ فِي غُرْبَتِهَا مِنَ الشَّدَائِدِ وَالضَّرْبِ وَالْجُوعِ وَالذُّلِّ وَالْهَوَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Nuzhata al-Zamāni ḥakat lahum jamīʿa mā jarā lahā maʿahu fī ghurbatihā mina al-shadāʾidi wa-al-ḍarbi wa-al-jūʿi wa-al-dhulli wa-al-hawāni
sentences.l: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān related to them all that befell her with him in her exile: of the hardships and the beating and the hunger and the abasement and the contempt.
sentences.i: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān told them all she had suffered at his hands in her exile: the hardships, the beatings, the hunger, the humiliation and the scorn.
sentences.n: ghurba, “being a stranger, exile far from home”. dhull and hawān, “abasement” and “contempt”, a near-synonym pair.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُمُ الْآنَ حَلَّ لِي قَتْلُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahumu al-āna ḥalla lī qatluhu
sentences.l: Then she said to them: Now his killing has become-lawful for me.
sentences.i: Then she said to them, “Now it is lawful for me to kill him.”
sentences.n: ḥalla, “to become lawful, permitted”; qatluhu, “his killing”, is its subject. lahumu: the pronoun takes a helping -u before the article.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَذَبَتِ السَّيْفَ وَقَامَتْ إِلَى الْبَدَوِيِّ لِتَقْتُلَهُ وَإِذَا هُوَ صَاحَ وَقَالَ يَامُلُوكَ الزَّمَانِ لَاتَدَعُوهَا تَقْتُلُنِي حَتَّى أَحْكِيَ لَكُمْ مَاجَرَى لِي مِنَ الْعَجَائِبِ
sentences.tr: thumma jadhabati al-sayfa wa-qāmat ilā al-badawiyyi li-taqtulahu wa-idhā huwa ṣāḥa wa-qāla yā mulūka al-zamāni lā tadaʿūhā taqtulunī ḥattā aḥkiya lakum mā jarā lī mina al-ʿajāʾibi
sentences.l: Then she drew the sword and rose toward the Bedouin to kill him; and behold, he cried-out and said: O kings of the time, do not leave her (to) kill me until I relate to you what befell me of the wonders!
sentences.i: Then she drew the sword and went at the Bedouin to kill him; but he cried out, “O kings of the age, do not let her kill me before I have told you the wonders that have befallen me!”
sentences.n: The print runs together yā mulūka, ياملوك, and lā tadaʿūhā, لاتدعوها. wa-idhā huwa ṣāḥa, “and suddenly he cried out”: idhā of surprise. lā tadaʿūhā taqtulunī, “do not leave her (to) kill me”: wadaʿa, “to leave, let”, followed by a bare imperfect. ḥattā aḥkiya, “until I tell”, subjunctive after ḥattā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا ابْنُ أَخِيهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَا عَمَّتِي دَعِيهِ يَحْكِي لَنَا حِكَايَةً وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَافْعَلِي مَاتُرِيدِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ibnu akhīhā Kāna Mā Kāna yā ʿammatī daʿīhi yaḥkī lanā ḥikāyatan wa-baʿda dhālika fa-ifʿalī mā turīdīna
sentences.l: And her brother's son, Kān Mā Kān, said to her: O my aunt, leave him (to) tell us a tale, and after that, do what you want.
sentences.i: Her nephew Kān Mā Kān said to her, “Aunt, let him tell us a story; afterwards do as you please.”
sentences.n: ʿamma, “paternal aunt”: Nuzhat al-Zamān is the sister of Kān Mā Kān's father Ḍawʾ al-Makān. daʿīhi yaḥkī, “leave him (to) tell”, the feminine imperative of wadaʿa, again with a bare imperfect. wa-baʿda dhālika fa-ifʿalī: a fa- before the imperative after a fronted time phrase. The print runs mā turīdīna, “what you want”, together as ماتريدين.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَتْ عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿat ʿanhu
sentences.l: And she turned-back from him.
sentences.i: So she drew back from him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمُلُوكُ الْآنَ احْكِ لَنَا حِكَايَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-mulūku al-āna iḥki lanā ḥikāyatan
sentences.l: And the kings said to him: Now relate to us a tale.
sentences.i: Then the kings said to him, “Now tell us a story.”
sentences.n: iḥki, “tell!”, the imperative of ḥakā, which loses its final long vowel.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا مُلُوكَ الزَّمَانِ إِنْ حَكَيْتُ لَكُمْ حِكَايَةً عَجِيبَةً تَعْفُوا عَنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā mulūka al-zamāni in ḥakaytu lakum ḥikāyatan ʿajībatan taʿfū ʿannī
sentences.l: And he said: O kings of the time, if I relate to you a wondrous tale, you-will-pardon me?
sentences.i: He said, “O kings of the age, if I tell you a wondrous tale, will you pardon me?”
sentences.n: taʿfū ʿannī, “you pardon me”: a jussive in the answer to in, “if”, written with the silent alif of the plural. Only the tone makes it a question.

sentences.t: قَالُوا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālū naʿam
sentences.l: They said: Yes.

sentences.t: فَابْتَدَأَ الْبَدَوِيُّ يُحَدِّثُهُمْ بِأَعْجَبِ مَا وَقَعَ لَهُ وَقَالَ اعْلَمُوا أَنِّي مِنْ مُدَّةٍ يَسِيرَةٍ أَرِقْتُ لَيْلَةً أَرَقًا شَدِيدًا وَمَا صَدَّقْتُ أَنَّ الصَّبَاحَ يُصْبِحُ
sentences.tr: fa-ibtadaʾa al-badawiyyu yuḥaddithuhum bi-aʿjabi mā waqaʿa lahu wa-qāla iʿlamū annī min muddatin yasīratin ariqtu laylatan araqan shadīdan wa-mā ṣaddaqtu anna al-ṣabāḥa yuṣbiḥu
sentences.l: And the Bedouin began telling them of the most-wondrous of what happened to him, and said: Know that I, a short while since, was-sleepless one night a sleeplessness severe, and did not believe that the morning would morning.
sentences.i: So the Bedouin began to tell them the most wonderful thing that had ever happened to him. Know, he said, that not long ago I lay awake one night, sleepless and restless, and could hardly believe that morning would ever come.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb takes bi- for the thing told. ariqtu … araqan shadīdan, “I was sleepless with a severe sleeplessness”, the cognate accusative again. mā ṣaddaqtu anna, “I did not believe that”: he could hardly wait for it. al-ṣabāḥ yuṣbiḥu, “the morning comes to morning”, a jingle on the root ṣ-b-ḥ, taken up again in the next sentence.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ قُمْتُ مِنْ وَقْتِي وَسَاعَتِي وَتَقَلَّدْتُ بِسَيْفِي وَرَكِبْتُ جَوَادِي وَاعْتَقَلْتُ رُمْحِي وَخَرَجْتُ أُرِيدُ الصَّيْدَ وَالْقَنَصَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu qumtu min waqtī wa-sāʿatī wa-taqalladtu bi-sayfī wa-rakibtu jawādī wa-iʿtaqaltu rumḥī wa-kharajtu urīdu al-ṣayda wa-al-qanaṣa
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, I rose from my time and my hour, and girded-myself with my sword, and mounted my steed, and couched my lance, and went-out wanting the hunt and the chase.
sentences.i: When morning came I rose that very hour, girded on my sword, mounted my horse, took up my lance and rode out to hunt and chase game.
sentences.n: min waqtī wa-sāʿatī, “from my time and my hour”: at once, there and then. taqallada bi-sayfihi, “to hang one's sword on by its baldric”; the shadda on تقلّدت is the print's. iʿtaqala rumḥahu, “to carry one's lance couched”, held between leg and stirrup, the rider's way of carrying it. ṣayd and qanaṣ, both “hunting”, a stock pair.

sentences.t: فَوَاجَهَنِي جَمَاعَةٌ فِي الطَّرِيقِ فَسَأَلُونِي عَنْ قَصْدِي فَأَخْبَرْتُهُمْ بِهِ فَقَالُوا وَنَحْنُ رُفَقَاؤُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-wājahanī jamāʿatun fī al-ṭarīqi fa-saʾalūnī ʿan qaṣdī fa-akhbartuhum bihi fa-qālū wa-naḥnu rufaqāʾuka
sentences.l: And a company met-me-face-to-face on the road, and they asked me about my aim, and I informed them of it; and they said: And we are your companions.
sentences.i: On the way a band of men met me and asked where I was bound. I told them, and they said, “Then we will ride with you.”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to inform (someone) of”: the verb takes bi- for the news. wa-naḥnu rufaqāʾuka, “and we are your companions”: we too will come along.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلْنَا كُلُّنَا مَعَ بَعْضِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-nazalnā kullunā maʿa baʿḍinā
sentences.l: And we went-down, all of us, with one-another.
sentences.i: So we all set off together.
sentences.n: maʿa baʿḍinā, “with one another”, colloquial for “together”. nazala usually means “to dismount, alight”, which cannot be meant here, since they ride on; it seems to mean “to go down (into the open country)”, to set out. The sense is doubtful.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ سَائِرُونَ وَإِذَا بِنَعَامَةٍ ظَهَرَتْ لَنَا فَقَصَدْنَاهَا فَنَفَرَتْ مِنْ بَيْنِ أَيْدِينَا وَهِيَ فَاتِحَةٌ أَجْنِحَتَهَا وَلَمْ تَزَلْ شَارِدَةً وَنَحْنُ خَلْفَهَا إِلَى الظُّهْرِ حَتَّى رَمَتْنَا فِي بَرِّيَّةٍ لَانَبَاتَ فِيهَا وَلَا مَاءَ وَلَمْ نَسْمَعْ فِيهَا غَيْرَ صَفِيرِ الْحَيَّاتِ وَزَعِيقِ الْجَانِّ وَصَرِيخِ الْغِيلَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu sāʾirūna wa-idhā bi-naʿāmatin ẓaharat lanā fa-qaṣadnāhā fa-nafarat min bayni aydīnā wa-hiya fātiḥatun ajniḥatahā wa-lam tazal shāridatan wa-naḥnu khalfahā ilā al-ẓuhri ḥattā ramatnā fī barriyyatin lā nabāta fīhā wa-lā māʾa wa-lam nasmaʿ fīhā ghayra ṣafīri al-ḥayyāti wa-zaʿīqi al-jānni wa-ṣarīkhi al-ghīlāni
sentences.l: And while we were going-along, behold, an ostrich appeared to us; and we made for it, and it shied-off from between our hands, spreading its wings, and did not cease fleeing, and we behind it, till the noon, until it cast us into a wilderness — no plant in it and no water — and we heard in it nothing but the hissing of the snakes and the shrieking of the jinn and the screaming of the ghouls.
sentences.i: As we rode along, an ostrich suddenly appeared before us. We gave chase, and it fled from under our very hands with its wings spread wide, and ran on and on with us behind it until noon, when it had drawn us into a wilderness without plant or water, where we heard nothing but the hiss of serpents, the shrieks of the jinn and the screams of the ghouls.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā bi-, “while … behold”: the bi- after idhā only marks what appears. fātiḥatun ajniḥatahā, “opening its wings”: the participle takes a direct object like its verb. The print runs lā nabāta, “no plant”, together as لانبات. jānn, the jinn as a race; ghīlān, plural of ghūl, the desert ogres said to lure travellers to their death. ramatnā fī, “it threw us into”: it led us astray into.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْنَا إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ غَابَتْ عَنَّا فَلَمْ نَدْرِ أَفِى السَّمَاءِ طَارَتْ أَمْ فِى الْأَرْضِ غَارَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalnā ilā dhālika al-makāni ghābat ʿannā fa-lam nadri a-fī al-samāʾi ṭārat am fī al-arḍi ghārat
sentences.l: And when we reached that place, it vanished from us; and we did not know: was it into the sky it flew, or into the earth it sank?
sentences.i: When we reached that spot it vanished from our sight, and we could not tell whether it had flown up into the sky or sunk down into the earth.
sentences.n: lam nadri, “we did not know”, jussive of darā, losing its final yāʾ. a- … am, “whether … or”; the fatḥa on the alif of اَفى is the print's own, marking the question, and فى is the print's spelling of fī. ṭārat / ghārat, “it flew / it sank”: rhymed prose. The ostrich, it seems, was no ordinary bird.

sentences.t: فَرَدَدْنَا رُؤُسَ الْخَيْلِ وَأَرَدْنَا الرَّوَاحَ ثُمَّ رَأَيْنَا أَنَّ الرُّجُوعَ فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ الشَّدِيدِ الْحَرِّ لَاخَيْرَ فِيهِ وَلَا إِصْلَاحَ
sentences.tr: fa-radadnā ruʾūsa al-khayli wa-aradnā al-rawāḥa thumma raʾaynā anna al-rujūʿa fī hādhā al-waqti al-shadīdi al-ḥarri lā khayra fīhi wa-lā iṣlāḥa
sentences.l: And we turned-back the heads of the horses and wanted the going-home; then we saw that the returning in this time, the intense of heat — no good in it and no setting-right.
sentences.i: So we turned our horses' heads and meant to go home; but then we judged that to turn back in such fierce heat would do no good and mend nothing.
sentences.n: rawāḥ, “going (home), setting out towards evening”. ruʾūs, “heads”, is written in the print without the wāw of the long vowel (Classical رؤوس). al-waqti al-shadīdi al-ḥarri, “the time intense of heat”: an adjective annexed to a noun. lā khayra fīhi wa-lā iṣlāḥa, “no good in it and no amending”, rhymes with al-rawāḥa. The print runs lā khayra together as لاخير.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اشْتَدَّ عَلَيْنَا الْحَرُّ وَعَطِشْنَا عَطَشًا شَدِيدًا وَوَقَفَتْ خُيُولُنَا فَأَيْقَنَّا بِالْمَوْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi ishtadda ʿalaynā al-ḥarru wa-ʿaṭishnā ʿaṭashan shadīdan wa-waqafat khuyūlunā fa-ayqannā bi-al-mawti
sentences.l: And the heat had grown-intense upon us, and we thirsted a severe thirst, and our horses stood-still; and we were certain of death.
sentences.i: The heat bore down on us, we were parched with thirst, and our horses stopped in their tracks, so that we gave ourselves up for dead.
sentences.n: ayqana bi-, “to be certain of”: the verb takes bi-. waqafat khuyūlunā, “our horses stood still”: they could go no further.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ كَذَلِكَ إِذْ نَظَرْنَا مِنْ بَعِيدٍ مَرْجًا أَفْيَحَ فِيهِ غِزْلَانٌ تَمْرَحُ وَهُنَاكَ خَيْمَةٌ مَضْرُوبَةٌ وَفِي جَانِبِ الْخَيْمَةِ حِصَانٌ مَرْبُوطٌ وَسِنَانٌ يَلْمَعُ عَلَى رُمْحٍ مَرْكُوزٍ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu ka-dhālika idh naẓarnā min baʿīdin marjan afyaḥa fīhi ghizlānun tamraḥu wa-hunāka khaymatun maḍrūbatun wa-fī jānibi al-khaymati ḥiṣānun marbūṭun wa-sinānun yalmaʿu ʿalā rumḥin markūzin
sentences.l: And while we were thus, lo, we beheld from afar a meadow wide-spreading, in it gazelles frisking; and there a tent pitched, and at the side of the tent a stallion tethered, and a spearhead gleaming on a lance planted-upright.
sentences.i: While we were in this plight we saw in the distance a broad meadow where gazelles were frisking, and there a tent was pitched, with a stallion tethered beside it and a spearhead glinting on a lance planted in the ground.
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … suddenly”. naẓara here takes a direct object: “to catch sight of”. afyaḥ, “wide, spacious”, of an open plain (diptote, so afyaḥa). khayma maḍrūba, “a pitched tent”: ḍaraba is the verb for pitching a tent. A lance planted upright by the door was the sign of a warrior's tent.

sentences.t: فَانْتَعَشَتْ نُفُوسُنَا مِنْ بَعْدِ الْيَأْسِ وَرَدَدْنَا رُؤُسَ خَيْلِنَا نَحْوَ تِلْكَ الْخَيْمَةِ نَطْلُبُ ذَلِكَ الْمَرْجَ وَالْمَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-intaʿashat nufūsunā min baʿdi al-yaʾsi wa-radadnā ruʾūsa khaylinā naḥwa tilka al-khaymati naṭlubu dhālika al-marja wa-al-māʾa
sentences.l: And our souls revived after the despair, and we turned the heads of our horses toward that tent, seeking that meadow and the water.
sentences.i: Our spirits revived after despair, and we turned our horses' heads toward the tent, making for the meadow and its water.
sentences.n: intaʿasha, “to revive, be refreshed”. naṭlubu, “seeking”, a bare imperfect describing how they went.

sentences.t: وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَيْهِ جَمِيعُ أَصْحَابِي وَأَنَافِي أَوَّلِهِمْ وَلَمْ نَزَلْ سَائِرِينَ حَتَّى وَصَلْنَا إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْمَرْجِ
sentences.tr: wa-tawajjaha ilayhi jamīʿu aṣḥābī wa-anā fī awwalihim wa-lam nazal sāʾirīna ḥattā waṣalnā ilā dhālika al-marji
sentences.l: And all my companions turned-toward it, and I in the first of them; and we did not cease going until we reached that meadow.
sentences.i: All my companions made for it, with me at their head, and we rode on until we came to the meadow.
sentences.n: The print runs anā fī, “I (was) in”, together as وانافي. ilayhi, “toward it”: the meadow. lam nazal sāʾirīna, “we did not cease going”: zāla takes its predicate in the accusative.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفْنَا عَلَى عَيْنٍ وَشَرِبْنَا وَسَقَيْنَا خُيُولَنَا فَأَخَذَتْنِي حَمِيَّةُ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafnā ʿalā ʿaynin wa-sharibnā wa-saqaynā khuyūlanā fa-akhadhatnī ḥamiyyatu al-jāhiliyyati
sentences.l: And we halted at a spring, and drank, and watered our horses; and the zealotry of the Ignorance seized me.
sentences.i: We halted at a spring, drank, and watered our horses; and then the old heathen fury took hold of me.
sentences.n: ʿayn, “eye”, is also a spring of water. ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyya, “the hot pride of the Age of Ignorance”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (48:26) for the reckless clan arrogance of pre-Islamic Arabia: Ḥammād owns that he acted as a lawless raider.

sentences.t: وَقَصَدْتُ بَابَ ذَلِكَ الْخِبَاءِ فَرَأَيْتُ فِيهِ شَابًّا لَانَبَاتَ بِعَارِضَيْهِ وَهُوَ كَأَنَّهُ هِلَالٌ وَعَنْ يَمِينِهِ جَارِيَةٌ هَيْفَاءُ كَأَنَّهَا قَضِيبُ بَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qaṣadtu bāba dhālika al-khibāʾi fa-raʾaytu fīhi shābban lā nabāta bi-ʿāriḍayhi wa-huwa ka-annahu hilālun wa-ʿan yamīnihi jāriyatun hayfāʾu ka-annahā qaḍību bānin
sentences.l: And I made for the door of that tent, and I saw in it a youth, no growth on his two cheeks, and he as-though he were a new-moon; and at his right a damsel slender-waisted, as-though she were a bough of willow.
sentences.i: I made for the entrance of that tent, and in it I saw a youth with not yet a hair upon his cheeks, like the new moon, and at his right hand a slender-waisted girl, like a bough of the ban tree.
sentences.n: The print runs lā nabāta, “no growth”, together as one word, لانبات; the phrase means he was still beardless. khibāʾ is a tent of wool or camel-hair, the same tent called khayma just before. hayfāʾ, “slender-waisted”, a diptote, and qaḍīb bān, “a bough of the ban (willow-like moringa)”, are stock praise of a beauty's tall, swaying form.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَعَتْ مَحَبَّتُهَا فِي قَلْبِي فَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الشَّابِّ فَرَدَّ عَلَيَّ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓartu ilayhā waqaʿat maḥabbatuhā fī qalbī fa-sallamtu ʿalā dhālika al-shābbi fa-radda ʿalayya al-salāma
sentences.l: And when I looked at her, love-of-her fell into my heart; and I greeted that youth, and he returned to me the greeting.
sentences.i: The moment I looked at her, love for her fell into my heart. I greeted the youth, and he returned my greeting.
sentences.n: waqaʿat maḥabbatuhā fī qalbī, “love of her fell into my heart”, the usual phrase for love at first sight. The shadda on عليّ is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ يَا أَخَا الْعَرَبِ أَخْبِرْنِي مَنْ أَنْتَ وَمَا تَكُونُ لَكَ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةُ الَّتِي عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu yā akhā al-ʿarabi akhbirnī man anta wa-mā takūnu laka tilka al-jāriyatu allatī ʿindaka
sentences.l: And I said: O brother of the Arabs, inform me who you are, and what is to you that damsel who is with you.
sentences.i: I said, “Brother Arab, tell me who you are, and what that girl with you is to you.”
sentences.n: yā akhā al-ʿarab, “O brother of the Arabs”, the courteous address of one Bedouin to another stranger of the desert. mā takūnu laka, “what is she to you”, asks her kinship: wife, sister or slave.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَ الشَّابُّ رَأْسَهُ إِلَي الْأَرْضِ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ وَقَالَ أَخْبِرْنِي مَنْ أَنْتَ وَمَا الْخَيْلُ الَّتِي مَعَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqa al-shābbu raʾsahu ilay al-arḍi sāʿatan thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu wa-qāla akhbirnī man anta wa-mā al-khaylu allatī maʿaka
sentences.l: And the youth lowered his head to the ground an hour, then he raised his head and said: Inform me who you are, and what are the horses that are with you.
sentences.i: The youth bowed his head to the ground for a while; then he raised it and said, “Tell me who you are, and what these horsemen with you are.”
sentences.n: aṭraqa raʾsahu, “he bowed his head”, in thought; sāʿatan, “an hour”, here only “a while”. The print spells ilā as الي, with yāʾ for the final alif maqṣūra. al-khayl, “the horses”, stands for the mounted men riding them.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ أَنَا حَمَّادُ بْنُ الْفَزَارِيِّ الْفَارِسِيُّ الْمَوْصُوفُ الَّذِى أُعَدُّ بَيْنَ الْعَرَبِ بِخَمْسِ مِائَةِ فَارِسٍ وَنَحْنُ خَرَجْنَا مِنْ مَحَلِّنَا نُرِيدُ الصَّيْدَ وَالْقَنَصَ فَأَدْرَكَنَا الْعَطَشُ فَقَصَدْتُ أَنَا بَابَ تِلْكَ الْخَيْمَةِ لَعَلِّي أَجِدُ عِنْدَكُمْ شَرْبَةَ مَاءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu anā Ḥammādu ibnu al-Fazāriyyi al-fārisiyyu al-mawṣūfu alladhī uʿaddu bayna al-ʿarabi bi-khamsi miʾati fārisin wa-naḥnu kharajnā min maḥallinā nurīdu al-ṣayda wa-al-qanaṣa fa-adrakanā al-ʿaṭashu fa-qaṣadtu anā bāba tilka al-khaymati laʿallī ajidu ʿindakum sharbata māʾin
sentences.l: And I said: I am Ḥammād son of al-Fazārī, the Fārisī, the described, who am counted among the Arabs as five hundred horsemen; and we went-out from our camping-place wanting the hunt and the chase, and thirst overtook us, so I made, I, for the door of that tent, that perhaps I might find with you a drink of water.
sentences.i: I said, “I am Ḥammād ibn al-Fazārī, al-Fārisī, the renowned, reckoned among the Arabs a match for five hundred riders. We rode out from our camp to hunt and course game, and thirst came upon us; so I made for the door of this tent, hoping to find a drink of water with you.”
sentences.n: The print has al-Fārisī, which would make this Bedouin of Fazāra “the Persian”; it may be a slip for al-fāris, “the horseman”, which the youth's answer (fāris maʿrūf wa-baṭal mawṣūf) seems to echo, but the reading is not certain, so the print is kept. al-Fazārī names the Arab tribe of Fazāra. alladhī uʿaddu, “who am counted”: the relative takes a first-person verb, agreeing with anā; the shadda on اعدّ is the print's, and الذى is written with dotless yāʾ. ʿadda bi-, “to reckon as equal to”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنِّي ذَلِكَ الْكَلَامَ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ الْمَلِيحَةِ وَقَالَ ائْتِي إِلَى هَذَا الرَّجُلِ بِالْمَاءِ وَمَاحَضَرَ مِنَ الطَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa minnī dhālika al-kalāma iltafata ilā al-jāriyati al-malīḥati wa-qāla iʾtī ilā hādhā al-rajuli bi-al-māʾi wa-mā ḥaḍara mina al-ṭaʿāmi
sentences.l: And when he heard from me that speech, he turned to the comely damsel and said: Come to this man with the water and what-is-at-hand of the food.
sentences.i: When he heard this from me, he turned to the lovely girl and said, “Bring this man water, and whatever food is at hand.”
sentences.n: iʾtī, feminine imperative of atā, “come”; atā bi-, “come with”, is “bring”. The print runs mā ḥaḍara, “what is present”, together as one word, ماحضر; mā ḥaḍara, “whatever is ready”, is the host's modest phrase for the meal he offers.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ تَسْحَبُ أَذْيَالَهَا وَالْحُجُولُ الذَّهَبُ تُشَخْشِخُ فِي رِجْلَيْهَا وَهِيَ تَتَعَثَّرُ فِي شَعْرِهَا وَغَابَتْ قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-jāriyatu tasḥabu adhyālahā wa-al-ḥujūlu al-dhahabu tushakhshikhu fī rijlayhā wa-hiya tataʿaththaru fī shaʿrihā wa-ghābat qalīlan
sentences.l: And the damsel rose, trailing her skirts, and the anklets, the gold, jingling on her two legs, and she stumbling in her hair; and she was-absent a little.
sentences.i: The girl rose, trailing her skirts, the golden anklets jingling about her feet, and stumbling over her own hair; and she was gone a little while.
sentences.n: ḥujūl, “anklets”; al-ḥujūlu al-dhahabu, “the anklets, the gold”, names the material by apposition. shakhshakha, “to jingle, rattle”, is a colloquial onomatopoeic verb. She trips on her hair, so long it reaches the ground: a stock hyperbole of beauty.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَتْ وَفِي يَدِهَا الْيُمْنَى إِنَاءٌ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ مَمْلُؤٌ مَاءً بَارِدًا وَفِي يَدِهَا الْيُسْرَى قَدَحٌ مَلْآنُ تَمْرًا وَلَبَنًا وَمَاحَضَرَ مِنْ لُحُومِ الْوُحُوشِ
sentences.tr: thumma aqbalat wa-fī yadihā al-yumnā ināʾun min fiḍḍatin mamluʾun māʾan bāridan wa-fī yadihā al-yusrā qadaḥun malʾānu tamran wa-labanan wa-mā ḥaḍara min luḥūmi al-wuḥūshi
sentences.l: Then she came-forward, and in her right hand a vessel of silver, filled with cold water, and in her left hand a bowl full of dates and milk and what-was-at-hand of the meats of the wild-beasts.
sentences.i: Then she came back, in her right hand a silver vessel filled with cold water, and in her left a bowl full of dates and milk and such game as there was.
sentences.n: mamluʾ, “filled”, is the print's spelling of mamlūʾ, with the hamza on wāw and no long vowel written. malʾān, “full”, a diptote, takes what fills it in the accusative, as does mamluʾ. luḥūm al-wuḥūsh, “the meats of wild beasts”, is game. Again the print runs mā ḥaḍara together as ماحضر.

sentences.t: فَمَا اسْتَطَعْتُ أَنْ آخُذَ مِنَ الْجَارِيَةِ طَعَامًا وَلَاشَرَابًا مِنْ شِدَّةِ مَحَبَّتِي لَهَا فَتَمَثَّلْتُ بِهَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ وَقُلْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā istaṭaʿtu an ākhudha mina al-jāriyati ṭaʿāman wa-lā sharāban min shiddati maḥabbatī lahā fa-tamaththaltu bi-hādhayni al-baytayni wa-qultu
sentences.l: And I could not take from the damsel food nor drink, from the intensity of my love for her; so I quoted-as-apt these two verses and said:
sentences.i: But I could take neither food nor drink from the girl's hands, so violent was my love for her; and I applied to her these two verses, saying:
sentences.n: The print runs wa-lā sharāban, “nor drink”, together as one word, ولاشرابا. tamaththala bi-, “to cite (verses) as fitting the case”.

sentences.t:
كَأَنَّ الْخِضَابَ عَلَى كَفِّهَا * غُرَابٌ عَلَى ثَلْجَةٍ وَاقِفُ
تَرَى الشَّمْسَ وَالْبَدْرَ مِنْ وَجْهِهَا * قَرِيبَيْنِ خَافٍ وَذَا خَائِفُ
sentences.tr:
ka-anna al-khiḍāba ʿalā kaffihā * ghurābun ʿalā thaljatin wāqifu
tarā al-shamsa wa-al-badra min wajhihā * qarībayni khāfin wa-dhā khāʾifu
sentences.l:
As-if the dye upon her palm * were a crow upon a snow-patch standing.
You see the sun and the full-moon from her face * near-together: (one) hidden, and this (one) afraid.
sentences.i:
The dye upon her palm is like * a raven standing on the snow.
In her face you see both sun and moon * close by: the one hides, the other fears.
sentences.n: The metre is mutaqārib, rhyming in -ifu. The print's pointing is kept as given. khiḍāb is a dye for the hands, henna or a darker tint, here dark against her white skin as a crow on snow. In the second line her face outshines both lights: the sun hides from it (khāfin, from khafiya, “to be hidden”) and the moon is afraid of it (khāʾif); khāfin and khāʾif make a near-pun.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لِلشَّابِّ بَعْدَ أَنْ أَكَلْتُ وَشَرِبْتُ يَا وَجْهَ الْعَرَبِ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي أَوْقَفْتُكَ عَلَى حَقِيقَةِ خَبَرِي وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ تُخْبِرَنِي بِحَالِكَ وَتُوقِفَنِي عَلَى حَقِيقَةِ خَبَرِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qultu li-al-shābbi baʿda an akaltu wa-sharibtu yā wajha al-ʿarabi iʿlam annī awqaftuka ʿalā ḥaqīqati khabarī wa-urīdu an tukhbiranī bi-ḥālika wa-tūqifanī ʿalā ḥaqīqati khabarika
sentences.l: Then I said to the youth, after I had eaten and drunk: O face of the Arabs, know that I have acquainted-you with the truth of my story, and I want you to inform me of your state and acquaint-me with the truth of your story.
sentences.i: Then, when I had eaten and drunk, I said to the youth, “O flower of the Arabs, I have told you the truth about myself; now I would have you tell me how things stand with you, and the truth of your story.”
sentences.n: wajh al-ʿarab, “face of the Arabs”, i.e. the best and foremost of them, a flattering address. awqafa ʿalā, “to make (someone) stand upon”, is “to acquaint with, inform of”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّابُّ أَمَّا هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ فَهِيَ أُخْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shābbu ammā hādhihi al-jāriyatu fa-hiya ukhtī
sentences.l: And the youth said: As for this damsel, she is my sister.
sentences.i: The youth said, “As for this girl, she is my sister.”

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ أُرِيدُ أَنْ تُزَوِّجَنِي بِهَا طَوْعًا وَإِلَّا أَقْتُلْكَ وَآخُذْهَا غَصْبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qultu urīdu an tuzawwijanī bihā ṭawʿan wa-illā aqtulka wa-ākhudhhā ghaṣban
sentences.l: And I said: I want you to marry me to her willingly, or-else I kill you and take her by-force.
sentences.i: I said, “I want you to give her to me in marriage of your own free will; otherwise I will kill you and take her by force.”
sentences.n: zawwaja bi-, “to give in marriage to”, with the woman after bi-; Classical also allows a direct object. wa-illā, “and if not”, stands for a condition, so the two verbs after it are pointed as its jussive apodosis. ṭawʿan … ghaṣban, “willingly … by force”, the usual pair.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَطْرَقَ الشَّابُّ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَفَعَ بَصَرَهُ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ لِي لَقَدْ صَدَقْتَ فِي دَعْوَاكَ أَنَّكَ فَارِسٌ مَعْرُوفٌ وَبَطَلٌ مَوْصُوفٌ وَأَنَّكَ أَسَدُ الْبَيْدَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika aṭraqa al-shābbu raʾsahu ilā al-arḍi sāʿatan thumma rafaʿa baṣarahu ilayya wa-qāla lī la-qad ṣadaqta fī daʿwāka annaka fārisun maʿrūfun wa-baṭalun mawṣūfun wa-annaka asadu al-baydāʾi
sentences.l: And at that the youth lowered his head to the ground an hour, then raised his gaze to me and said to me: Truly you have spoken-true in your claim that you are a horseman well-known and a champion renowned, and that you are the lion of the desert.
sentences.i: At that the youth bowed his head to the ground a while; then he lifted his eyes to me and said, “You have spoken truly in claiming to be a famous horseman and a renowned champion, the lion of the desert.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: maʿrūf / mawṣūf. The shadda on اليّ is the print's. al-baydāʾ, “the waterless waste”, the desert.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ إِنْ هَجَمْتُمْ عَلَيَّ غَدْرًا وَقَتَلْتُمُونِي قَهْرًا وَأَخَذْتُمْ أُخْتِي فَإِنَّ هَذَا يَكُونُ عَارًا عَلَيْكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin in hajamtum ʿalayya ghadran wa-qataltumūnī qahran wa-akhadhtum ukhtī fa-inna hādhā yakūnu ʿāran ʿalaykum
sentences.l: But if you fall upon me in-treachery, and kill me by-force, and take my sister, then this will be a shame upon you.
sentences.i: But if you fall upon me treacherously, overpower and kill me and take my sister, that will be a disgrace to you.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: ghadran / qahran. He now speaks to Ḥammād and his band together, in the plural. The shadda on عليّ is the print's.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ كُنْتُمْ عَلَى مَا ذَكَرْتُمْ مِنْ أَنَّكُمْ فُرْسَانٌ تُعَدُّونَ مِنَ الْأَبْطَالِ وَلَاتُبَالُونَ بِالْحَرْبِ وَالنِّزَالِ فَأَمْهِلُونِي قَلِيلًا حَتَّى أَلْبَسَ آلَةَ حَرْبِي وَأَتَقَلَّدَ بِسَيْفِي وَأَعْتَقِلَ رُمْحِي وَأَرْكَبَ فَرَسِي وَأَصِيرَ أَنَا وَإِيَّاكُمْ فِي مَيْدَانِ الْحَرْبِ
sentences.tr: wa-in kuntum ʿalā mā dhakartum min annakum fursānun tuʿaddūna mina al-abṭāli wa-lā tubālūna bi-al-ḥarbi wa-al-nizāli fa-amhilūnī qalīlan ḥattā albasa ālata ḥarbī wa-ataqallada bi-sayfī wa-aʿtaqila rumḥī wa-arkaba farasī wa-aṣīra anā wa-iyyākum fī maydāni al-ḥarbi
sentences.l: And if you are as you have mentioned, that you are horsemen counted among the champions, and you care not for war and combat, then grant-me-respite a little, until I put on my war-gear, and gird myself with my sword, and couch my lance, and mount my horse, and I and you come to be in the field of war.
sentences.i: And if you are what you have said, horsemen counted among the champions, who care nothing for war and single combat, then give me a little time, until I put on my armour, gird on my sword, couch my lance and mount my horse, and you and I stand together on the field of battle.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-abṭāl / al-nizāl. The print runs wa-lā tubālūna, “and you do not care”, together as one word, ولاتبالون. taqallada, “to gird on (a sword)”, normally takes its object directly; here it takes bi-. anā wa-iyyākum, “I and you”: iyyā carries the pronoun after wa- as if after maʿa, “with”.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ ظَفِرْتُ بِكُمْ أَقْتُلْكُمْ عَنْ آخِرِكُمْ وَإِنْ ظَفِرْتُمْ بِي وَقَتَلْتُمُونِي فَهَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ أُخْتِي لَكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-in ẓafirtu bikum aqtulkum ʿan ākhirikum wa-in ẓafirtum bī wa-qataltumūnī fa-hādhihi al-jāriyatu ukhtī lakum
sentences.l: Then if I prevail over you, I kill you to the last of you; and if you prevail over me and kill me, then this damsel, my sister, is yours.
sentences.i: If I get the better of you, I will kill you to the last man; and if you get the better of me and kill me, then this girl, my sister, is yours.”
sentences.n: ẓafira bi-, “to win, prevail over”. ʿan ākhirikum, “to the last of you”, i.e. every one.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ مِنْهُ هَذِهِ الْكَلَامَ قُلْتُ لَهُ إِنَّ هَذَا هُوَ الْإِنْصَافُ وَمَا عِنْدَنَا خِلَافٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu minhu hādhihi al-kalāma qultu lahu inna hādhā huwa al-inṣāfu wa-mā ʿindanā khilāfun
sentences.l: And when I heard from him this (fem.) speech, I said to him: This, it is the fairness, and there is not with us a disagreement.
sentences.i: When I heard these words from him, I said to him, “That is fair dealing, and we have no quarrel with it.”
sentences.n: hādhihi al-kalām, “this speech”: the print sets the feminine demonstrative before the masculine kalām, as the edition does now and then; it is kept as printed, for Middle Arabic often treats such collective nouns as feminine. inṣāf, “fairness, giving each his due”. mā ʿindanā khilāf, “we have no objection”, literally “there is no disagreement with us”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَدَدْتُ رَأْسَ جَوَادِى إِلَى خَلْفِي وَقَدْ زَادَ بِى الْجُنُونُ فِي مَحَبَّةِ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى أَصْحَابِي وَوَصَفْتُ لَهُمْ حُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا وَحُسْنَ الشَّابِّ الَّذِي عِنْدَهَا وَشَجَاعَتَهُ وَقُوَّةَ جَنَانِهِ وَكَيْفَ يَذْكُرُ أَنَّهُ يُصَادِمُ أَلْفَ فَارِسٍ
